intro: The Ridgid HD1400 NXT is the best wet/dry shop vacuum for most garages and home workshops: a 14-gallon tank, a 2-1/2-inch hose that swallows chips without clogging, a drain port for water and filters you can buy almost anywhere. For floods and renovation debris the larger Craftsman 16-gallon is the better fit, and for cars and small spills a compact DeWalt or Shop-Vac is easier to carry.

The two numbers printed biggest on a shop vac box, gallons and peak horsepower, say little about how it will clean. Hose diameter, airflow, filtration and how easily the tank empties decide that. Below are seven picks ranked by job, then plain answers on suction, sizing, filters, water pickup and cordless models.
quickAnswer: Buy the Ridgid HD1400 NXT for a typical garage or workshop. Step up to the Craftsman CMXEVBE17595 for regular water and renovation cleanup, choose the Vacmaster Beast for a built-in blower, and add a compact DeWalt DXV06P or Shop-Vac 5989300 for cars. Woodworkers who sand indoors should look at the Fein Turbo II extractor.

blocks.p: **Short answer:** the Ridgid HD1400 NXT is the best wet/dry shop vacuum for most garages and home workshops. It pairs a 14-gallon tank with a 2-1/2-inch hose and a drain port, and its filters and bags are stocked at nearly every home center.

blocks.p: Choose by the mess you clean most. Flooded basements and renovation debris call for the bigger Craftsman. Fine dust from sanding indoors calls for an extractor like the Fein. Car interiors and quick spills call for a compact DeWalt or Shop-Vac, ideally alongside a full-size vac rather than instead of one.

Every rating below comes from the maker's published specs, warranty terms and recurring owner feedback. Peak horsepower is listed because makers print it, but as the sections further down explain, hose diameter and airflow tell you much more.

sections.h: The 7 Best Wet/Dry Shop Vacuums in 2026, Ranked

blocks.p: The 14-gallon NXT is the vac most garages should start with. Ridgid rates its motor at 6.0 peak horsepower and fits it with a 2-1/2-inch hose, the diameter that swallows wood chips, leaves, gravel and drywall scraps without jamming. Fourteen gallons means you are not emptying it every few minutes, yet it still tucks under a workbench. The drain port near the base lets you empty water into a floor drain instead of tipping a heavy, sloshing drum. Ridgid sells fine-dust cartridges, HEPA-rated filters and dust bags for it, and attachments are easy to find in stores. Ridgid backs its wet/dry vacs with a limited lifetime warranty. Like most universal-motor vacs it is loud, and onboard accessory storage is basic.
**Pros:** wide hose resists clogs; drain port for water; filters and bags sold almost everywhere; limited lifetime warranty.
**Cons:** loud under load; basic accessory storage; bulky on stairs.

blocks.h3: Best for Big Messes: Craftsman CMXEVBE17595

blocks.p: When the job is volume, such as a wet basement, a garage cleanout or a demolition day, the 16-gallon Craftsman earns its size. Craftsman rates it at 6.5 peak horsepower with a 2-1/2-inch hose, and the bigger drum means fewer trips to empty water. A blower port reverses the airflow for clearing leaves off a patio or dust out of corners, and the kit includes a spread of nozzles. Size is the trade-off: a full tank of water is very heavy, so use the drain port, and plan for floor space. For small workbench cleanups, a smaller vac with the same hose is easier to live with.
**Pros:** large drum for water and debris; 2-1/2-inch hose; blower port; strong capacity for the money.
**Cons:** heavy when full; loud; more vac than a small shop needs.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Craftsman+CMXEVBE17595&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best Value With a Blower: Vacmaster Beast VJH1211PF

blocks.p: The Beast's motor head lifts off and becomes a handheld blower, which you will use more than you expect: clearing sawdust off a table saw, blowing leaves out of a garage or drying a wet floor. Vacmaster rates it at 5.5 peak horsepower with a 12-gallon tank and a 2-1/2-inch hose, which covers most garage and workshop jobs. It ships with a cartridge filter, and owners commonly suggest adding a bag for fine dust. Casters and a handle make it easy to roll. Some accessories feel light-duty, but the mix of capacity, hose size and blower is hard to beat at its price tier.
**Pros:** detachable blower; wide hose on a mid-size tank; strong value; rolls easily.
**Cons:** some flimsy accessories; cartridge alone is weak on fine dust; loud as a blower.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Vacmaster+Beast+VJH1211PF&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best Cordless: Milwaukee M18 FUEL 6 Gallon Wet/Dry Vac

blocks.p: This is the vac for people who already carry M18 batteries and need to clean where a cord is a nuisance: job sites, vehicles, far corners of a property. It uses a brushless motor and ships with a filter suited to fine dust. Suction and runtime depend on the pack, and high-output batteries make a clear difference. It picks up water like corded models, though the smaller tank and battery limit how much you can move per session. As a sole home-shop vac it costs more and does less than a corded unit with a wider hose; as a second vac for an M18 owner, it is very convenient.
**Pros:** no cord; brushless M18 motor; fine-dust filtration; rugged build.
**Cons:** expensive without existing packs; runtime tied to battery size; smaller tank.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Milwaukee+M18+FUEL+wet+dry+vac+6+gallon&tag=sktiger-20)

DeWalt's 6-gallon DXV06P is light enough to carry in one hand, which makes it the one to grab for cars, stairs, upstairs bathrooms and small spills. DeWalt rates it at 4.0 peak horsepower, and the poly tank will not dent or rust if water sits in it. It includes a cartridge filter, car-friendly nozzles and a blower port. The smaller hose and tank clog and fill quickly on chips or renovation debris, so it is not a workshop vac. As a companion to a larger machine, or the only vac in an apartment or condo, it is a sensible pick.
**Pros:** one-hand carry; rust-proof poly tank; good for vehicles; blower port.
**Cons:** narrow hose clogs on debris; small tank on wet jobs; not for shop duty.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=DeWalt+DXV06P&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best for Fine Dust: Fein Turbo II

blocks.p: The Fein Turbo II is a dust extractor, built to plug into sanders, routers, track saws and multi-tools and catch dust at the source. Its auto-start outlet switches the vac on and off with the tool, with a short run-on to clear the hose. It runs quieter than typical shop vacs, accepts fleece bags and HEPA filtration, and uses a narrower hose sized for tool ports. That makes it excellent for finishing work, cabinet building and drywall sanding. It costs far more than a shop vac, and the small hose is poor at floor debris such as chips and gravel.
**Pros:** auto-start outlet; quieter running; HEPA and fleece bag options; superb at sanding dust.
**Cons:** much higher price; tool-port hose, not bulk debris; overkill for garage cleanup.

sections.h: What Shop Vac Has the Best Suction?

blocks.p: The vac with the best suction for your job is the one with the most airflow through the widest hose you need, not the biggest horsepower number. Of the picks here, the Craftsman 16-gallon and the Ridgid HD1400 carry the highest peak ratings with 2-1/2-inch hoses, which is why they lead for garage debris and water.

Peak horsepower describes motor output for an instant with no load, a condition that never happens while you vacuum. The fan, housing and hose shape decide how much of that power reaches the nozzle, so two vacs with identical peak ratings can perform very differently. Treat the figure as a rough size class only.

blocks.h3: What CFM and water lift tell you

ul: **Airflow (CFM)** is the volume of air moved. High airflow lifts light, bulky material such as sawdust, leaves and drywall dust.
**Sealed suction (water lift, in inches)** is how hard the motor pulls against a blocked opening. High water lift helps with heavy debris, water and long hose runs.

blocks.p: When a maker publishes both, you finally have something real to compare. Rough targets for a mid-size corded vac: 100 or more CFM for everyday cleanup and 50 or more inches of water lift for liquids. Treat these as rules of thumb, because some brands quote CFM at the motor rather than at the end of the hose.

blocks.h3: Features that make a vac pleasant to own

blocks.p: A drain port, casters that roll over cords, a place to wrap hose and cord, a blower port, and filters a nearby store actually stocks. If replacement filters are hard to find, you end up running a clogged one, and a clogged filter cripples suction faster than any motor weakness.

sections.h: What Size Hose and Tank Do You Need?

blocks.p: Get a 2-1/2-inch hose for garage and workshop debris, then the smallest tank that handles your water and debris volume.

blocks.p: A narrow hose moves less air at higher speed, so it feels punchy at the nozzle and pulls dust from upholstery well. A wide hose moves more air and passes bulky material. Many woodworkers keep the wide hose for floors and an adapter or second hose for tool dust ports. Hose length matters too: every extra foot, bend and adapter steals airflow, so roll the vac closer rather than adding hose. Chip-heavy tools need the wide hose; our [benchtop planer guide](/best-benchtop-planer/) explains why a planer overwhelms anything narrower.

ul: **2.5 to 5 gallons:** cars, apartments, small spills.
**6 to 9 gallons:** one-car garage, small shop, general household use.
**12 to 16 gallons:** two-car garage, frequent renovation, water pickup.
**Over 16 gallons:** contractors and homes that flood regularly.

blocks.h3: How heavy does a full tank get?

blocks.p: Water weighs about 8.3 pounds per gallon, so a large tank full of water can weigh far more than you want to lift. The float switch stops airflow before the drum is truly full, but on any vac used for water often, a drain port is a must.
Many households end up with two: a mid-size or large corded vac for the garage, plus a compact one for the car. That pair often costs less than one premium vac and is more convenient.

sections.h: Do You Need a HEPA Filter or a Bag for Fine Dust?

blocks.p: Yes, for drywall, concrete or sanding dust. A standard paper cartridge catches sawdust and dirt but lets fine dust through, so the vac blows it back into the room. For fine material, fit a fine-dust cartridge or HEPA-rated filter and add a collection bag inside the tank.

A bag catches most of the fine dust before it reaches the filter. The filter stays cleaner, suction lasts longer, and emptying the tank stops being a dust storm. Pair a bag with a fine-dust or HEPA filter for drywall sanding and concrete grinding.

Cutting or grinding concrete, stone, brick and mortar releases crystalline silica, a serious lung hazard. OSHA's construction silica standard calls for HEPA-filtered vacuums for cleanup in many situations, and homeowners doing the same work should follow similar habits: a fitted respirator rated for the dust, no dry sweeping, and HEPA vacuum cleanup. Grinding a slab before coating it, covered in our [garage floor epoxy guide](/best-garage-floor-epoxy/), is one of the most common cases.

Tap it out over a trash can outdoors, or blow compressed air from the clean side outward while wearing a mask. Replace filters that are torn, caked beyond recovery or water-damaged, and keep a spare so you can swap and keep working.

sections.h: Shop Vac or Dust Extractor: Which Do You Need?

blocks.p: Buy a shop vac for general cleanup and an extractor only if you sand, rout or cut indoors often.

A shop vac picks up almost anything, including water and bulky debris, from floors and surfaces. A dust extractor plugs into a power tool and captures fine dust as it is made. Extractors run quieter, filter better and usually have an auto-start outlet.

If you regularly sand cabinet parts, furniture or trim indoors, catching dust at the tool keeps the air and every surface cleaner than sweeping up afterward, and it protects finishes from settling dust.

blocks.h3: When a shop vac is the better buy

blocks.p: For garage cleanup, car interiors, water and the occasional pile of sawdust, a shop vac does more for far less money. Fitted with a fine-dust filter and a bag, and connected to tools through an adapter, it handles occasional tool dust reasonably well.

Those tools make chips, not dust. For long sessions, a dust collector with a large hose is the right tool. For occasional use, a shop vac with a 2-1/2-inch hose and a cyclone separator can keep up with a small benchtop planer. If you are choosing a battery platform that includes a cordless vac, our [Milwaukee vs DeWalt comparison](/milwaukee-vs-dewalt/) covers the trade-offs.

sections.h: How Do You Pick Up Water With a Shop Vac?

blocks.p: Remove the paper filter, fit a foam sleeve or the wet filter your maker specifies, and plug into a GFCI-protected outlet. Check that the float in the filter cage moves freely, because it shuts off airflow when the tank is full so water never reaches the motor. When the motor pitch suddenly rises and suction drops, the float has closed and the tank needs emptying.

Keep the plug connection off wet floors and never run the vac in water deep enough to reach the motor housing or cord. If a basement has flooded deeply, or water has reached outlets or appliances, shut off power at the panel and have a professional assess it first. Once the water is out, a [basement dehumidifier](/best-dehumidifier-for-basement/) helps dry what the vac cannot reach.

blocks.h3: What never goes in a shop vac

ul: Gasoline, solvents, paint thinner or any flammable liquid, because the motor can ignite vapors.
Hot ashes or embers, which can smolder in the tank for hours.
Toxic materials, unless the vac is specifically rated for them.

blocks.p: Empty and rinse the tank, wipe out the float cage, and let everything dry with the lid off. A tank sealed with water inside grows mildew. Rinse the hose and hang it to drain. If the garage doubles as a car-care bay, the vac pairs well with a pressure washer and a [surface cleaner](/best-surface-cleaner-for-pressure-washer/) for the floor.

sections.h: Why Is My Shop Vac Losing Suction?

blocks.p: Almost always a clogged filter. In rough order of likelihood, the causes are a clogged filter, a full tank or closed float, a blockage in the hose or nozzle, a loose lid or missing gasket, and a hole in the hose. Work through them in that order before blaming the motor.

Pull the hose off and feel the suction at the tank inlet. Strong pull there means the clog is in the hose or nozzle; push a broom handle through the hose or drop a small object through it to find the jam. Weak pull at the inlet points to the filter, float, lid seal or motor.

blocks.h3: Why fine dust chokes filters so fast

blocks.p: Without a bag, a cartridge used on drywall dust can lose most of its airflow within minutes. A bag or a cyclone separator on fine material prevents most of that.

ul: **Cyclone separator:** sits between hose and vac, usually on a bucket, and spins debris out before it reaches the filter. The single best add-on for sawdust and chips.
**Auto-start switch:** turns the vac on with your power tool. Check that tool and vac together do not exceed the circuit; two 15-amp loads on one 15-amp circuit will trip the breaker.
**Smooth-wall, crush-resistant hose:** loses less airflow than a ribbed one.

blocks.h3: When the motor is the problem

blocks.p: A strained sound, hot smell or sparks through the vents mean stop and inspect. Universal-motor brushes wear out, and some vacs let you replace them; on budget models, replacing the vac often makes more sense.

sections.h: Are Cordless Shop Vacs Worth It?

blocks.p: Only for specific jobs, or if you already own the batteries. Corded vacs still deliver the most sustained airflow for the money and can run through an hour-long garage cleanout without fading.

blocks.h3: Where a battery vac earns its place

blocks.p: Vehicles, where dragging a cord around a truck is awkward; job sites and outbuildings with no power; and quick cleanups, because grabbing a cordless vac beats unwinding a cord, so the mess gets handled right away.

blocks.h3: Does it make sense without the batteries?

blocks.p: Bare cordless vacs from the big tool brands are fairly priced, but adding high-capacity packs and a charger can roughly double the outlay. If you already run Milwaukee, DeWalt, Ryobi or Makita, a bare vac is an easy add. If you are choosing a platform from scratch, our [Ryobi tools review](/ryobi-tools-review/) covers the budget option many homeowners start with.

blocks.h3: How long does a battery vac run?

blocks.p: It varies with pack size and load. Expect a useful session of spot cleaning and vehicle work from a large pack, not a whole-garage cleanout. Wet pickup drains batteries faster, and cold garages cut capacity, so keep a second charged pack nearby.

mistakes: Leaving the paper filter in for water

A paper cartridge soaks up water, sags, grows mildew and chokes airflow so the motor strains. Remove the dry filter before any wet job and fit a foam sleeve or the wet filter your manual names. Let the tank and cage dry completely before the paper filter goes back on.
Vacuuming drywall dust without a bag

Drywall and concrete dust slip through ordinary filters and coat the room, and what the filter catches blinds it within minutes. Use a collection bag with a fine-dust or HEPA filter for these jobs. The bag traps most of the dust, keeps suction steady and makes emptying far cleaner.
Shopping by gallons instead of hose size

A big tank behind a narrow hose jams on chips and leaves that a smaller vac with a wide hose clears easily. In a garage or shop, a 2-1/2-inch hose matters more than extra capacity. Choose the hose first, then the smallest tank that fits your water and debris volume.
Vacuuming hot ash or flammable liquids

Embers can smolder inside the tank for hours and start a fire after the vac is put away. Gasoline, solvents and thinner give off vapors the motor can ignite. Wait until ash is completely cold and use a metal ash vacuum, and soak up flammable spills with absorbent instead.
Ignoring the filter until suction dies

A dust-caked filter can cut airflow drastically, and owners often blame the motor. Tap the filter clean after dusty jobs, keep a spare to swap in, and replace any cartridge that is torn or water-damaged. A clean filter is the cheapest way to make an old vac perform like new.
bottomLine: The Ridgid HD1400 NXT is the right wet/dry shop vacuum for most garages and workshops thanks to its 2-1/2-inch hose, drain port, manageable 14-gallon tank and easy-to-find filters. Move up to the Craftsman 16-gallon for frequent water and renovation work, pick the Vacmaster Beast if a blower would earn its keep, keep a compact DeWalt or Shop-Vac for cars, and consider the Fein Turbo II if you sand indoors. Whatever you buy, judge it by hose and airflow, match the filter to the dust, pull the paper filter before water, and keep flammables and hot ash out of the tank.

faqs.q: What is the best wet dry shop vacuum?
faqs.a: The Ridgid HD1400 NXT is the best wet/dry shop vacuum for most homes. Its 14-gallon tank, 2-1/2-inch hose, drain port and widely stocked filters suit garages and workshops. The Craftsman 16-gallon is better for frequent water and renovation debris, and a compact DeWalt DXV06P is better for cars and small spills.

faqs.q: What shop vac has the best suction?
faqs.a: Look for the highest airflow through a 2-1/2-inch hose rather than the biggest peak horsepower. Among these picks, the Craftsman 16-gallon and Ridgid HD1400 carry the strongest ratings with wide hoses. When makers publish them, compare CFM for light debris and water lift for heavy material and liquids, since peak horsepower is a no-load figure.

faqs.q: What size shop vac do I need for a garage?
faqs.a: A 12 to 14-gallon vac with a 2-1/2-inch hose suits most two-car garages and home workshops. A 6 to 9-gallon vac is enough for a one-car garage or small shop, and 16 gallons or more makes sense if you clear water or renovation debris often. Bigger tanks are heavier and harder to store.

faqs.q: Do I need a HEPA filter on a shop vac?
faqs.a: Only for fine dust. Use a HEPA-rated filter with a collection bag when cleaning drywall dust, concrete or masonry dust, or fine sanding dust. Concrete and masonry dust contain silica, and OSHA construction rules call for HEPA vacuums in many cleanup tasks. For sawdust, dirt and water, a standard filter works.

faqs.q: Can a shop vac pick up water from a flooded basement?
faqs.a: Yes, if the water is shallow. Remove the paper filter, fit a foam sleeve, use a GFCI outlet, keep the cord connection dry and empty through the drain port when the float shuts off airflow. If water is deep or near outlets and appliances, shut off power at the panel and call a professional first.

faqs.q: Are cordless shop vacs as good as corded?
faqs.a: Not for sustained cleanup. Corded vacs deliver more continuous airflow for the money and run as long as you need. Cordless vacs such as the Milwaukee M18 FUEL make sense for vehicles, job sites and quick cleanups, especially if you already own the batteries. Without packs on the shelf, a corded vac is the better buy.

faqs.q: Why does my shop vac lose suction?
faqs.a: A clogged filter is the most common cause. After that, check for a full tank that has closed the float, a blockage in the hose or nozzle, a loose lid or missing gasket, and a split hose. Remove the hose and feel suction at the tank inlet to narrow it down before suspecting the motor.
